title: Nixon-Era Laws, Harry Potter, and the Russian Email That Skeeved Me Out
author: Jacob Carr
source: What Teachers Have to Say (whatteachershavetosay.substack.com), August 20, 2026
summary: Teacher Jacob Carr sets out to translate the legal architecture of student data privacy for classroom teachers, arguing that IT department pushback on new apps is rarely arbitrary but rather the visible edge of decades-old federal and state law. He walks through FERPA's 1974 origin and its 'school official exception,' which lets ed-tech vendors handle student data only if they meet four strict conditions, and shows how AI-era 'de-identification' claims collapse in practice, illustrated by his own demonstration that a room of educators could identify his son from three anonymized traits. Carr then covers COPPA's under-13 consent requirement and the industry's workaround of setting AI platform age floors at 18, a state-by-state patchwork of privacy laws in California, New York, Illinois, and Texas, and the deeper risk posed by generative AI's tendency to memorize and later reproduce training data, citing research showing models can be prompted to output large fractions of copyrighted books verbatim. The piece closes by reframing student data privacy as a matter of classroom management and digital ethics rather than a bureaucratic IT inconvenience.
points: Carr's live demonstration, identifying his own son from just three 'de-identified' traits in front of a room of educators, offers a concrete, memorable proof that de-identification is 'purely performative theater' under modern AI, not just an abstract legal risk.

He explains the FERPA 'school official exception' mechanism precisely: vendors gain temporary school-staff status only if they meet four conditions (real staff work, direct control, need-to-know access, zero side hustles), and violating any one collapses the entire legal shield.
His personal Pimsleur anecdote, ads following a private staff email into his personal Facebook feed, demonstrates that district-protected communication is not the sealed vault most educators assume.

Carr flags a specific and actionable compliance trap: teachers signing up for 'free' AI tools like Claude for Teachers using an institutional email creates a 'legal void' because individual sign-up bypasses the district contract that would otherwise establish FERPA's required direct control.

The Harry Potter extraction research he cites, that targeted prompts can pull over 90 percent of a copyrighted novel verbatim from a trained model, is used to argue that any sensitive student writing or IEP notes fed into an unvetted AI tool carries a real, demonstrated resurfacing risk, not a hypothetical one.
quotes: Every time an IT department skuttles a software request without explanation, what's happening is that you're actually staring at a giant, toothy legal machine grinding away beneath our classrooms.
Legally, FERPA states data is not de-identified if a reasonable person in the school community could figure out who wrote it. Modern machine learning shatters that standard without flinching.
Eight people raised their hands and positively identified my son by name. De-identified does not stop something from being easily re-identified, especially with the power of AI behind the task.
When a splash page screams "FERPA Compliant," laugh. FERPA binds educational institutions. It literally cannot bind a private software vendor.

By using targeted extraction prompts, researchers pulled over 90 percent of entire copyrighted books like Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone word for word, while image diffusion models have been caught faithfully reconstructing private, copyrighted photos directly from their training sets.
They are likely doing the grueling, unglamorous work of standing between your students and a multi-billion-dollar data extraction engine that views classroom work as free training material.
In this new era, protecting student privacy is no longer just an IT headache. It is classroom management. It is digital ethics.
